messages.author: acb848005b4fc0c3
messages.subject: Interfacing with renjin
parts:
Hi all,

I´m implmenting a Multidimensional Array (MDArray) in JRuby.  MDArray is similar to numpy but for the Ruby/Java platform.  I just came across of Renjin and I was wondering if there is any good way of interfacing MDArray with Renjin.

MDArray is based on two libraries: NetCDF-Java and Parallel Colt.  NetCDF is a library and model for storing and retrieving large scientific datasets.  MDArray uses NetCDF at this point mostly for its multidimensional array library, but is also able to write NeCDF 3 files (up to 2TB).  Parallel Colt is a very nice library for scientific computation and linear algebra.  Integrating NetCDF and Parallel Colt was quite easy as both libraries store data on a one-dimensional java array and use indexes to simulate multidimensions.

Now, if this same datastore (one dimensional java array) could be viewed somehow by Renjin as an R dataset, then the integration would be easy and this could be a very strong library.  How is data stored in Renjin?  Could it view a one dimensional java array as a dataset for R?

Thanks, 

--
Rodrigo Botafogo

messages.author: f06db63329fab1f9
messages.subject: Re: Interfacing with renjin
parts:
Sounds great!

Renjin has a layer of abstraction between R code and data storage, so you could easily expose your MDArray as an R object.

If your underlying storage is indeed a one dimensional java array, in column-major order, then it is as simple as:

AttributeMap attributes = AttributeMap.builder().setDim(numRows, numCols).build();
DoubleVector matrix = DoubleArrayVector.unsafe(myArray, attributes);

If you have more than two dimensions, use :
int dim[] = {3, 5, 9, 4 };  //etc
AttributeMap attributes = AttributeMap.builder().setDim(new IntVector(dim)).build();

If the array is very large, you can use the unsafe() factory method to create the DoubleVector without creating a copy of the array. But you have to guarantee that the matrix won't change, as Renjin assumes that it can lazily defer operations on large vectors.

You can also provide your own DoubleVector implementation, for sparse matrices, for example, where you can organize the underlying storage as you need. The DistanceMatrix object is a good example of this:

https://github.com/bedatadriven/renjin/blob/master/core/src/main/java/org/renjin/DistanceMatrix.java

I should also note that in principle referencing a 2TB matrix using a DoubleVector facade over a NetCDF file should be no problem, as Renjin will defer operations on large data objects until usually a reduce operation like sum() or mean(), but there are still some basic operations for which still aren't set up to defer operations properly, and they might try to create a copy of your 2TB matrix, which will fail. For example, this *will* work:

x <- mMdArrayJavaClass$readCdf("2tbmatrix.dat")
y <- t(x / 2)
print(dim(y))
print(y[3000,4000])

because y just contains a basically a wrapper that says: when someone asks for element i,j, grab j,i from x and divide by two. 

however, I don't believe rbind() is set up to defer operations, so 

z <- rbind(x, x) 

will probably try to allocate a java array of 4tb, which won't succeed. 

Also, vectors in Renjin are currently limited by 32-bit (actually 31-bit) indices, so the total logical size of a matrix is limited. We need to think a bit about the best way to do this: GNU R has introduced 64-bit indices, but R itself still only has 64-bit floating point numbers and 32-bit signed integers, so you still can't fully address the large vectors, at least from R code. 

I think what might be interesting for Renjin is just to make the R "integer" type a 64-bit signed integer, and then 64-bit indices follow naturally, but I'm not sure what impact if any this will have on performance. 

Anyway, if you hit any obstacles, let me know and I'll see what we can do quickly to eliminate the bottleneck. 

Best,
Alex

messages.author: 3b104dc6686d0c85
messages.subject: Re: Interfacing with renjin
parts:
Rodrigo,

R stores everything as a vector (or array in C parlance). It knows two classes of objects for multi-dimensional arrays: "matrix" and "array". Both are created by simply setting the "dim" attribute to either a length 2 integer vector (for a matrix) or a length 3+ integer vector (for arrays). For example:

x <- seq(9) # x is a simple vector
dim(x) <- c(3,3) # create a 3x3 matrix
class(x) # returns "matrix"

y <- seq(8)
dim(y) <- c(2,2,2) # create a 2x2x2 array
class(y) # returns "array"

You can see in Alex' example that he is actually doing the same in Java: setting the dim attribute in the AttributeMap.

Dimensions are not often labelled in R, but if they are then these names are stored in the "dimnames" attribute. Since dimensions are explicitly defined in NetCDF files, you could use that information to create this attribute in the R matrix/array.

Maarten-Jan

because y just contains a basically a wrapper that says: when someone asks for element i,j, grab j,i from x and divide by two. 

however, I don't believe rbind() is set up to defer operations, so 

z <- rbind(x, x) 

will probably try to allocate a java array of 4tb, which won't succeed. 

Also, vectors in Renjin are currently limited by 32-bit (actually 31-bit) indices, so the total logical size of a matrix is limited. We need to think a bit about the best way to do this: GNU R has introduced 64-bit indices, but R itself still only has 64-bit floating point numbers and 32-bit signed integers, so you still can't fully address the large vectors, at least from R code. 

I think what might be interesting for Renjin is just to make the R "integer" type a 64-bit signed integer, and then 64-bit indices follow naturally, but I'm not sure what impact if any this will have on performance. 

Anyway, if you hit any obstacles, let me know and I'll see what we can do quickly to eliminate the bottleneck.
